items.sentence_raw: Bullying can take a variety of forms, from the verbal - being taunted or called hurtful names - to the physical - being kicked or shoved - as well as indirect forms, such as being excluded from social groups.
A survey I conducted with Irene Whitney found that in British primary schools up to a quarter of pupils reported experience of bullying, which in about one in ten cases was persistent.
items.explain: Q27: Students often confuse this section with just listing types of bullying, but look at the numbers — the passage says *'a quarter of pupils reported experience of bullying'* and *'one in ten cases was persistent'*. This is a **survey** about how **common** bullying is. So the heading is **iv** — *Research into how common bullying is in British schools*.

items.sentence_raw: There was less bullying in secondary schools, with about one in twenty-five suffering persistent bullying, but these cases may be particularly recalcitrant.

Q31: The question asks about **secondary schools**, and the passage directly compares them to primary schools. It says *'There was less bullying in secondary schools'* — **'less'** is the opposite of **'more'**. So the answer is **B** — there was less bullying than in primary schools.

items.sentence_raw: Bullying is clearly unpleasant, and can make the child experiencing it feel unworthy and depressed.
items.explain: Q28: This section is not about how often bullying happens, but what it does to children. The passage says bullying makes a child feel *'unworthy and depressed'* and victims have *'difficulties with interpersonal relationships as adults'*. These are all **effects** on the children. So the heading is **vi** — *The effect of bullying on the children involved*.

items.sentence_raw: In extreme cases it can even lead to suicide, though this is thankfully rare.

Victimised pupils are more likely to experience difficulties with interpersonal relationships as adults, while children who persistently bully are more likely to grow up to be physically violent, and convicted of anti-social offences.

It says they are more likely to have *'difficulties with interpersonal relationships as adults'* — **'interpersonal relationships'** means **'forming relationships'**. So the answer is **D** — they may have difficulty forming relationships in later life.

items.sentence_raw: Until recently, not much was known about the topic, and little help was available to teachers to deal with bullying.

The passage says *'not much was known about the topic, and little help was available'* — this shows a **lack of knowledge and resources**. The denial was a result of this lack, not just a lie. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: "There is no bullying at this school" has been a common refrain, almost certainly untrue.
Fortunately more schools are now saying: "There is not much bullying here, but when it occurs we have a clear policy for dealing with it."
Three factors are involved in this change.
items.explain: Q30: This section explains why schools changed their approach — it lists *'Three factors'* like new **awareness** and new **resources**. These are **developments** that led to a new way of dealing with bullying. So the heading is **vii** — *Developments that have led to a new approach by schools*.

items.sentence_raw: First is an awareness of the severity of the problem.

items.sentence_raw: Second, a number of resources to help tackle bullying have become available in Britain.

items.sentence_raw: For example, the Scottish Council for Research in Education produced a package of materials, "Action Against Bullying", circulated to all schools in England and Wales as well as in Scotland in summer 1992, with a second pack, "Supporting Schools Against Bullying", produced the following year.
In Ireland, "Guidelines on Countering Bullying Behaviour in Post-Primary Schools" was published in 1993.
Third, there is evidence that these materials work, and that schools can achieve something.
This comes from carefully conducted 'before and after' evaluations of interventions in schools, monitored by a research team.
In Norway, after an intervention campaign was introduced nationally, an evaluation of forty-two schools suggested that, over a two-year period, bullying was halved.
items.explain: Q34: The passage says in Norway, after a campaign, *'bullying was halved'* — **'halved'** means reduced by **50%**. This directly matches option **A**. ***Option B is a trap*** — the passage mentions forty-two schools, not twenty-one. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: The Sheffield investigation, which involved sixteen primary schools and seven secondary schools, found that most schools succeeded in reducing bullying.

Evidence suggests that a key step is to develop a policy on bullying, saying clearly what is meant by bullying, and giving explicit guidelines on what will be done if it occurs, what records will be kept, who will be informed, what sanctions will be employed.
items.explain:
Q35: The passage says *'a key step is to develop a policy on bullying'* — the question asks for the most important step, and **'key step'** means the same thing. So the answer is **policy**.

Q36: The passage says the policy should give *'explicit guidelines on what will be done if it occurs'* — the question asks for detailed instructions on how to react. **'Guidelines'** are exactly that — detailed instructions. So the answer is **guidelines**.

items.sentence_raw: The policy should be developed through consultation, over a period of time - not just imposed from the head teacher's office!
Pupils, parents and staff should feel they have been involved in the policy, which needs to be disseminated and implemented effectively.
Other actions can be taken to back up the policy.
There are ways of dealing with the topic through the curriculum, using video, drama and literature.
items.explain: Q37: The question asks where action can be taken besides the policy, and the passage says *'ways of dealing with the topic through the curriculum'* — this is useful for *'raising awareness'*. So the answer is **curriculum**.

items.sentence_raw: These are useful for raising awareness, and can best be tied in to early phases of development, while the school is starting to discuss the issue of bullying.
items.explain: Q37: The question asks where action can be taken besides the policy, and the passage says *'ways of dealing with the topic through the curriculum'* — this is useful for *'raising awareness'*. So the answer is **curriculum**.

items.sentence_raw: They are also useful in renewing the policy for new pupils, or revising it in the light of experience.
But curriculum work alone may only have short-term effects; it should be an addition to policy work, not a substitute.
There are also ways of working with individual pupils, or in small groups.

Assertiveness training for pupils who are liable to be victims is worthwhile, and certain approaches to group bullying such as 'no blame', can be useful in changing the behaviour of bullying pupils without confronting them directly, although other sanctions may be needed for those who continue with persistent bullying.
items.explain: Q38: The question talks about training potential targets of bullying, and the passage says *'pupils who are liable to be victims'* — **'liable to be'** means **'potential'**. These pupils get **assertiveness training** to be more self-confident. So the answer is **victims**.

items.sentence_raw: Work in the playground is important, too.
One helpful step is to train lunchtime supervisors to distinguish bullying from playful fighting, and help them break up conflicts.
items.explain: Q39: The question asks what supervisors must distinguish bullying from, and the passage says they must *'distinguish bullying from playful fighting'*. The exact words are right there. So the answer is **playful fighting**.

items.sentence_raw: Another possibility is to improve the playground environment, so that pupils are less likely to be led into bullying from boredom or frustration.
With these developments, schools can expect that at least the most serious kinds of bullying can largely be prevented.
items.explain: Q40: The whole passage moves from describing the problem to showing how schools can **prevent** bullying — the last section says serious bullying *'can largely be prevented'*. This is a shift from just managing crises to stopping them before they start. So the best title is **D** — *Bullying: from crisis management to prevention*.

items.sentence_raw: The more effort put in and the wider the whole school involvement, the more substantial the results are likely to be.
The reduction in bullying - and the consequent improvement in pupil happiness - is surely a worthwhile objective.

subtitles: Persistent bullying is one of the worst experiences a child can face. How can it be prevented? Peter Smith, Professor of Psychology at the University of Sheffield, directed the Sheffield Anti-Bullying Intervention Project, funded by the Department for Education. Here he reports on his findings.
